newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Rushdie marks eight years under fatwah.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Rushdie marks eight years under fatwah.

text.p: British writer Salman Rushdie on Friday marked the eighth anniversary of his life in hiding by condemning Europe's "tokenist" effort to pressure Iran into withdrawing its death threat.

"The extreme passivity of the Foreign Office has permitted the rest of the EU (European Union) to go to sleep on this issue, and has given the Iranians the sign that there is really no need for them to do very much at all," Rushdie wrote in the Guardian newspaper. "A few stiff words once a year are no substitute for policy."

Just this week, an increased bounty of $2.5 million was offered for Rushdie's life, eight years after the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini imposed the "fatwa", or death edict, that upturned Rushdie's life.
Yet Rushdie reserved his real anger for the Western world, saying "the EUs response to such threats has been little more than tokenist. It has achieved, in one word, nothing.
"Iran is under very little (I would even say, no) pressure on this matter. But for eight years, some of us have been under a fair amount of stress," he wrote.
Iranian officials say the edict is purely a religious matter that government cannot withdraw.

The death sentence was issued for Rushdie's alleged blasphemy against Islam in his book "The Satanic Verses". Since then, Rushdie has lived under 24-hour police protection, although in the past year he has appeared more often in public.
The Indian-born author said he hoped to see more aggressive British action on his behalf in the months ahead.
But Rushdie, known as a leftwing socialite on London's literary scene, placed his main hopes on the likely election of Labour leader Tony Blair as Britain's next prime minister.
An election is due by May 22, with Labour riding some 20 points ahead of the ruling Conservatives in opinion polls.

"Today, on this tawdry anniversary, I ask Mr Blair to come to the aid of this one particular artist. As he knows, and has been good enough to tell me, the principles involved go far beyond the survival of a single individual," Rushdie said.

Days after the Foreign Office condemned the increased bounty on Rushdie's head, the Times newspaper said Britain nevertheless planned to sponsor a stand at an energy fair in Tehran, encouraging firms to invest in Iran's oil and gas sector.

It quoted a Foreign Office aide as saying there was no contradiction in promoting British trade in Iran at a time when political relations were deteriorating. "Critical dialogue" was still the EU's policy towards Iran.
